To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
TB is stigmatised and this stigma is perceived to be a barrier to effective TB control.
the stigma associated TB has come full circle in South Africa.
the stigma associated to tuberculosis in a time when HIV and AIDS is rampant has changed from the past when it is seen as a Xhosa disease to the present when it is associated with HIV and AIDS.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social construction of TB as a ‘disease of the poor’.
the manner in which the stigma associated with HIV/AIDS has impacted on the perception and control of TB, a disease which has been endemic for many years in the Eastern Cape.
the social construction of TB and its relationship to AIDS in South Africa.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
TB has become stigmatised again, and that this stigma is a major barrier to TB control.
the stigma associated to TB is not as strong as it was in the past, but is still present in a form that may hinder the control of the disease.
TB is not stigmatised per se.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stigma attached to TB is complex and dynamic and that it is not only a matter of the disease itself, but also of how the public understands the causes of the disease and how it can be cured.

TB is perceived as a serious, potentially fatal condition that can be cured if the prescribed course is followed and that the spread of TB is mainly attributed to the irresponsible behaviour and non-compliance of TB patients.
stigma and discrimination are not only a barrier to the control of TB, but also a barrier to the fight against HIV/AIDS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stigma is not a static phenomenon but a dynamic process that can be modified by the way in which the public is educated and the media reports the disease.
TB and HIV are inextricably intertwined in the Eastern Cape and that stigma and discrimination associated with TB is likely to have a negative impact on the fight against TB.
stigma and discrimination have a direct impact on the health-seeking behaviour of TB patients.
